item.summary: This journal entry synthesizes the current status of the responsibility formation project, emphasizing the formal governance role of ethics-based auditing and the structural challenges posed by autonomy. The research revises the notebook on accountability in automated decision-making to incorporate recently collected evidence regarding the intersection of cognitive decline and automated data gathering, as well as broader conceptual frameworks of autonomy.

claims.statement: Ethics-based auditing (EBA) serves as a structured governance mechanism that formalizes accountability by requiring documentation at intervention points.

support.explanation: Identifies the core operational definition of EBA within the context of automated decision systems.
support.passage: In this article, we outline the conditions under which EBA procedures can be feasible and effective in practice. First, we argue that EBA is best understood as a ‘soft’ yet ‘formal’ governance mechanism.

actions.findings: Ethics-based auditing (EBA) serves as a structured governance mechanism that formalizes accountability by requiring documentation at intervention points. [source-f4b920d1d52f4115]
actions.limitations: Requires empirical validation of intervention point effectiveness in diverse organizational contexts; does not resolve the philosophical ambiguity of 'responsibility' for machines.
actions.next_questions: How can EBA frameworks scale to systems where automated decision-making processes are opaque or highly dynamic?
actions.reason: Revision incorporating new evidentiary support for governance and autonomy.
actions.summary: Ethics-based auditing (EBA) provides a formal, though 'soft', governance framework for automated decision systems. While autonomy is complex, EBA helps bridge the gap between automated outputs and decision-subject justifications by mandating consistent documentation and ethical deliberation at key intervention points.
actions.title: Ethics-Based Auditing as a Governance Mechanism for Automated Systems
